title: The path, closed
hook: eight factors, walked together, not one after another

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth jhana, and your line, wrapped in white. Did you meet one pleasant and one unpleasant moment with the same even attention? Day four hundred.

Forty-eight days ago, this stretch began with a wheel of eight spokes, and a nun named Dhammadinna sorting the eight into three trainings. Since then we've taken the spokes out one at a time and looked at each: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. That's how you learn a list. But a wheel doesn't turn one spoke at a time, and the suttas don't describe the path that way either. Today the spokes go back in. Today: the path, closed.
screen: `FORTY-EIGHT DAYS AGO: ONE WHEEL.` → `EIGHT SPOKES, ONE AT A TIME.` → `TODAY THEY GO BACK IN.`

segments.voice: Here are the eight once more: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. At the start, Dhammadinna showed how they sort into virtue, concentration and wisdom. Today the Great Forty, MN 117, shows how they feed each other. In one who has right view, the Buddha says, right intention comes into being. In one with right intention, right speech. From right speech, right action; from right action, right livelihood; and on down the line, each factor giving rise to the next, as far as right concentration. And there the sutta keeps going. In one with right concentration, right knowledge comes into being, and in one with right knowledge, right liberation. Eight factors for the one in training; ten for the one who has arrived. The same sutta has view, effort and mindfulness running around each of the others, so the chain isn't a ladder you climb once. Nobody finishes right view before starting right speech. You speak a little more carefully, and your view clears a little. Your view clears, and your work changes. Your work changes, and the mind gathers more easily. The Dhammapada says it in one line, in Max Müller's translation: “The best of ways is the eightfold.” The Pali word for path, magga, is the ordinary word for a road. And a road isn't walked with all the left steps first, then all the right. Both feet, the whole way.
screen: `VIRTUE, CONCENTRATION, WISDOM.` · `EACH FACTOR GIVES RISE TO THE NEXT.` · `TEN FOR THE ONE WHO HAS ARRIVED.` · `BOTH FEET, THE WHOLE WAY.` · then, large: `EIGHT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the eight pass through, one breath each. First breath: view, seeing things as they are. Second: intention, goodwill. Third: speech, the words you'll use today. Fourth: action, harming no one. Fifth: livelihood, your work. Sixth: effort, the good you'll keep going. Seventh: mindfulness, this breath. Eighth: concentration, gathered here. Then let go of the list, and sit with all eight at once, nothing left out. The bell holds the time.
The path. Eight factors, walked together like the spokes of one wheel, each one strengthening the rest.
Your line: eight together. Today, pick one ordinary task and count how many of the eight are already in it. Day four hundred.

howItsDone: Buddhists across schools teach the eight factors as three trainings, virtue, concentration and wisdom, developed together rather than in sequence; the eight-spoked wheel is widely used as a symbol of the teaching.

pairs: path: the ordinary word for a road

myth: the eight factors are mastered strictly in order, one by one
they're walked together; each strengthens the others.
in MN 117, the chain stops at right concentration
it goes on to right knowledge and right liberation: ten factors for one who has arrived.
in MN 44, a nun explains the path's three trainings
Dhammadinna, and the Buddha says he'd have answered the same.

fork.setup: in MN 117, the Buddha says one factor leads the way for the others. which one?
fork.reveal: right view comes first. in one with right view, right intention comes into being, and so on down the line, each factor giving rise to the next.

original.note: Pali ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo: the noble eightfold path; aṅga means a limb or factor, not a step.

trapdoor: what you thought: eight steps, climbed one after another.
what it means: eight factors developed together, each supporting the rest.

what a scholar hears: aṅga means a limb, a factor, not a rung; MN 117 calls right view the forerunner and adds right knowledge and right liberation, ten factors for the arahant; MN 44 groups the eight into sīla, samādhi and paññā.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 44, Culavedalla Sutta (Dhammadinna and the three trainings)
Majjhima Nikaya 117, Mahacattarisaka Sutta (right view comes first)

sources.quoted: The best of ways is the eightfold

notes: Dhammapada 273 opening ('The best of ways is the eightfold') quoted from Max Müller (1881) from memory; please check against the 1881 text.
